strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and relatively underexplored setting: neural multi-objective routing on directed multigraphs, where both the next node and the parallel edge must be selected.
The two proposed architectures offer a useful quality-efficiency tradeoff: GMS-EB directly constructs edge sequences, while GMS-DH learns to prune parallel edges before faster node-based decoding.

The experimental study is unusually broad for this topic, covering MOTSP, MOCVRP, multigraph MOTSP, a time-window variant, multiple graph distributions and sizes, and zero-shot scaling to larger graphs and more parallel edges.

Results consistently show that the proposed models substantially outperform the neural baseline and evolutionary methods on asymmetric and multigraph instances. GMS-DH is particularly attractive in runtime, while GMS-EB generally provides higher solution quality.

Comparisons include strong single-objective heuristics, several evolutionary algorithms, specialized neural baselines, runtime measurements, training-cost analysis, and an ablation of learned versus deterministic pruning.
The presentation is generally clear, with explicit architectural descriptions, training equations, complexity discussion, and substantial supplementary detail.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is entirely synthetic despite strong real-world motivation. The multigraph distributions are especially stylized and explicitly do not satisfy the triangle inequality, limiting conclusions about road-network routing or other practical multigraphs.

The claimed broad applicability is stronger than demonstrated: experiments are limited to bi-objective, dense directed graphs and a small set of routing formulations. The main multigraph benchmark has additive edge costs, for which exact preference-dependent pruning is already available; only the time-window experiment genuinely requires more contextual edge selection.

The strongest solver, LKH with scalarization, remains better on essentially all MOTSP and MGMOTSP benchmarks. Thus, the contribution is primarily a speed-quality tradeoff rather than superior solution quality, and augmented GMS-EB can itself become relatively slow.

Important reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including how the ideal point used in Chebyshev scalarization is obtained, the precise normalized-hypervolume transformation, the preference distribution during training, and full hypernetwork specifications. Code is promised only after acceptance.

Results report means over test instances but no variability across instances, confidence intervals, significance tests, or independent training seeds. This makes small reported differences—often below one percentage point—hard to interpret.

Runtime comparisons mix GPU neural inference with CPU heuristic execution and therefore do not provide a clean compute-normalized comparison. Training is also expensive, reaching roughly 1.7 hours per epoch for GMS-EB on the reported multigraph setting.

The learned-pruning ablation is narrow. On the additive MGMOTSP, learned and exact simple pruning perform almost identically, while the stronger benefit is shown only on one synthetic time-window construction. More ablations of the encoder, joint-training objective, sample counts, conditioning mechanism, and pruning accuracy would better isolate the contribution.

The GMS-DH selection objective substitutes the unavailable optimal downstream tour with the best of samples from the simultaneously trained routing policy. The resulting biased and nonstationary training signal is intuitively motivated but receives little analysis of stability or failure modes.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant and comparatively underexplored setting: neural multi-objective routing on multigraphs, where both the next node and the connecting edge must be selected.
The edge-based and dual-head formulations are sensible. In particular, the learned pruning head offers a useful speed–quality trade-off, while the direct edge decoder retains routing context.

The experiments cover multiple routing problems, graph sizes, synthetic distributions, zero-shot scaling, inference times, and both neural and evolutionary baselines. The proposed models generally outperform the included learned baselines, sometimes by large margins.

weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is limited to randomly generated complete graphs. The paper explicitly notes that its multigraph distributions do not satisfy the triangle inequality, and it provides no road-network, logistics, or established multigraph benchmark despite motivating the work through real transportation applications. It is therefore unclear whether the reported gains transfer to the intended setting.

The decisive MGMOTSPTW comparison is not convincing. MBM is handicapped by an acknowledged ad hoc linear pre-pruning rule, the evolutionary implementations are described as non-central and perform very poorly, and no strong problem-specific solver, constrained-search method, or multigraph routing heuristic is included. Consequently, the large gains in Table 3 do not establish state-of-the-art solution quality.

On the additive MGMOTSP, Proposition 1 makes exact preference-dependent pruning straightforward, and LKH remains better than every proposed model. Thus, much of the evaluation demonstrates faster approximate amortized inference rather than superior optimization, while the genuinely nontrivial time-window case receives only two synthetic distributions at sizes 20 and 50.

The architectural novelty is moderate: the method largely combines GREAT, multi-pointer decoding, hypernetwork conditioning, POMO, and REINFORCE. Predicting edges directly is natural, and the dual-head model is interesting, but the paper provides too little isolation of which components are responsible for its performance.

The ablation study is narrow. It mainly compares learned and simple pruning, without controlled ablations of the multigraph encoder, preference conditioning, scalar-cost term, selection-head depth, curriculum, pretraining, sampling budgets, or the max-over-rollouts reward used for the selection head.

Reporting only mean hypervolume over 200 instances, with no repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests, makes small claimed improvements—often below one percentage point—difficult to interpret. The definition of normalized hypervolume is also incomplete, and essential training details such as the preference distribution and ideal point used for Chebyshev scalarization are not clearly specified.

The efficiency presentation excludes the very large training cost: GMS-EB reportedly requires up to 1.7 hours per epoch while training uses roughly 200 epochs and 100,000 generated instances per epoch. Describing the method as sample-efficient based on epoch curves is consequently misleading, and no amortization analysis is provided.

Reproducibility is presently insufficient: code is promised only after acceptance, random seeds and variability are absent, and several implementation choices needed to reproduce the objectives and evaluation are underspecified. Overall, the promising formulation is not supported by sufficiently realistic or rigorous evidence for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem: neural multi-objective routing on asymmetric multigraphs, where the model must select both the next node and the connecting edge.

The two proposed architectures are complementary and technically sensible. GMS-EB directly models edge actions, while GMS-DH introduces learned pruning to obtain substantially better scalability; the associated tradeoff is clearly analyzed.

The empirical study is broad in problem size and synthetic distribution, covering MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, and a time-window variant. It includes strong classical solvers, evolutionary algorithms, a neural baseline, augmentation results, ablations, runtime measurements, training behavior, and zero-shot tests.

Results consistently support the central empirical claims. GMS is substantially stronger than the neural and evolutionary baselines on asymmetric instances, remains within a few percent of LKH where LKH applies, and performs especially well on the multigraph time-window task where simple edge pruning is inadequate.

The learned-versus-simple-pruning ablation is informative: it shows that learned edge selection matters for the nonlinear time-window objective, while simple pruning can suffice for the additive MGMOTSP case.
The presentation is generally clear, with well-motivated architectures, explicit training objectives, useful diagrams, and unusually extensive supplementary experiments.
weaknesses: The practical motivation is stronger than the realism of the evaluation. All multigraph instances are synthetic, dense, and generated from independent edge attributes; the authors explicitly note that these distributions do not satisfy the triangle inequality. No road-network, logistics, or other real-world multigraph data are evaluated.

Evidence for the most important difficult setting, MGMOTSPTW, is comparatively limited. The classical baselines either ignore time windows, rely on a custom weak evolutionary implementation, or use an intentionally mismatched linear pruning rule. Consequently, the large performance margin does not conclusively establish competitiveness against a strong problem-specific heuristic.

The paper reports means over test instances but no uncertainty, multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly relevant for reinforcement learning and for several comparatively small differences between model variants.

Several essential reproducibility details appear unspecified: the preference distribution used in training, ideal points and any objective normalization used for Chebyshev scalarization, the precise normalization of hypervolume, random seeds, and some decoding details. Code is only promised after acceptance.

The evaluation is restricted to two objectives. This leaves the claimed general multi-objective applicability insufficiently tested, especially because preference coverage and hypernetwork conditioning become more challenging as the number of objectives increases.

The main MGMOTSP task admits exact per-preference edge pruning under linear scalarization, reducing how strongly it demonstrates the necessity of learning directly on multigraphs. The time-window experiment addresses this concern, but only through a single simplified synthetic task.

GMS-EB is computationally expensive, scaling as O(MN^4), and its augmented inference can approach or exceed the classical baseline's runtime. Training is also costly—up to roughly 1.7 hours per epoch in the reported multigraph setting—limiting practical reuse.

Novelty is meaningful but primarily architectural: the method combines an existing GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoding, hypernetwork conditioning, POMO-style reinforcement learning, and learned pruning. The paper offers limited new theoretical understanding beyond the straightforward linear-pruning proposition.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting: neural multi-objective routing directly on multigraphs and asymmetric graphs.
Proposes two complementary designs with a sensible quality-efficiency tradeoff: direct edge-based construction and learned edge pruning followed by node-based routing.
The evaluation is broad, covering TSP and CVRP variants, time windows, multiple graph distributions, 20–200 nodes, additional parallel edges, three objectives, and zero-shot generalization.

Comparisons include strong classical solvers, evolutionary algorithms, and several adapted neural architectures. The proposed methods are consistently stronger than the neural baselines on asymmetric and multigraph tasks while remaining much faster than high-quality classical solvers.
The learned-versus-simple-pruning and pre-pruning ablations provide useful evidence for the selection head, particularly on the time-window problem where local linear pruning is inadequate.
The method and training objectives are presented clearly, and the extensive appendix supplies meaningful architecture, data-generation, baseline, and runtime details.
weaknesses: All multigraph experiments use synthetic, dense, fully connected distributions. No real road-network multigraph or established multigraph-routing benchmark is evaluated, so the claimed practical relevance remains largely unverified.

The strongest evidence for learned pruning comes from MGMOTSPTW, but its baselines are weak: LKH and OR-Tools merely ignore the time windows, MBM uses an acknowledged naive pruning rule, and no competitive problem-specific time-window heuristic is included.

Results are reported only as averages over one test set, with no variability, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or results across independent training seeds. This is important because several reported improvements are small.

Important reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous, including the ideal point used for Chebyshev rewards and the precise normalization applied to hypervolume. No code or trained-model availability is stated.

Runtime comparisons mix GPU neural inference with CPU heuristic execution, and do not incorporate the substantial training cost. GMS-EB requires up to roughly 1.7 hours per epoch on the reported multigraph setting, weakening its efficiency narrative unless inference is heavily amortized.

The complexity argument appears inconsistent: given the stated scoring of only outgoing edges, N construction steps, and N POMO rollouts, edge decoding appears to scale as O(MN^3), rather than the claimed O(MN^4). The paper should derive encoder, memory, and decoder costs separately.

The architectural novelty is moderate: the work mainly combines an existing GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoding, hypernetwork conditioning, POMO training, and a task-specific pruning head. Its novelty rests substantially on adapting these ingredients to a new problem representation.

GMS-DH degrades as the number of edges or objectives grows in some settings, and the experiments do not establish scalability to realistic sparse graphs with heterogeneous or variable numbers of alternatives beyond small synthetic tests.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and comparatively underexplored problem: neural multi-objective routing on multigraphs, where both node order and parallel-edge choice must be determined.

The two proposed designs are sensible and complementary: GMS-EB directly selects edges, while GMS-DH trades some flexibility for substantially faster inference through learned pruning and node-based routing.

The empirical study is broad in terms of problem variants, graph sizes, objective counts, synthetic distributions, classical heuristics, evolutionary algorithms, and neural baselines. The larger-instance tests and learned-versus-simple-pruning ablation are useful.
The manuscript is generally clear and technically organized, and it candidly reports the high training cost of the edge-based model.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately support the paper's real-world motivation. All multigraph experiments use dense synthetic FLEX/FIX generators with independent random edge attributes; these generators do not satisfy the triangle inequality and do not resemble road-network multigraphs. No real or realistically simulated transportation network is evaluated.

The strongest claimed result, on MGMOTSPTW, lacks a convincing baseline. The implicit LKH/OR-Tools variants ignore time windows, MBM prunes using travel time rather than the actual violation-count objective, and the evolutionary methods perform extremely poorly. Thus, the large reported advantage does not establish competitiveness against a strong problem-specific solver.

Comparisons are confounded by scalarization choices. GMS is principally trained with Chebyshev rewards, whereas several strong classical and neural baselines use linear scalarization. Linear scalarization cannot recover unsupported Pareto solutions, so hypervolume differences may reflect the decomposition method rather than the proposed architecture. A matched Chebyshev or otherwise comparable baseline is needed.

There is no uncertainty analysis: results appear to use one trained model per setting, with no multiple training seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Many reported differences are below one percentage point and therefore cannot be interpreted reliably.

Important reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including how the Chebyshev ideal values are obtained, exactly how hypervolume is normalized, complete solver configurations and stopping budgets, and code/checkpoint availability. Training can require hundreds of GPU-hours, making these omissions consequential.

The stated complexity analysis for GMS-EB appears inconsistent. If only outgoing edges are scored, there are O(MN) candidates per step, O(N) steps, and O(N) POMO trajectories, suggesting O(MN^3) decoding rather than the claimed O(MN^4). This weakens a central motivation for GMS-DH and should be corrected or rigorously derived.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the contributions of the learned selection head, shared encoder, post-encoding pruning, reward choice, and extra transformer layers. On MGMOTSP, learned and simple post-encoder pruning perform almost identically, so the benefit of learned pruning is demonstrated mainly on one weakly benchmarked problem.

The paper's generalization evidence is limited to larger instances from essentially the same generators. It does not test distribution shift, sparse graphs, variable or heterogeneous numbers of parallel edges, correlated edge attributes, or realistic time-window dynamics. The assumption that vehicles never wait when arriving early is also nonstandard and limits practical interpretation.

Presentation has minor but visible issues, including a stray double-asterisk in the abstract and misleading emphasis that boldfaces the best results only after excluding the strongest LKH/HGS baselines. Overall, the work is promising and likely technically plausible, but the evaluation and reproducibility gaps place it marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem: neural multi-objective routing directly on multigraphs, where both node order and parallel-edge selection must be decided.

The two proposed architectures offer a sensible quality-efficiency tradeoff: GMS-EB performs direct edge-level construction, while GMS-DH uses learned pruning followed by more scalable node-level routing.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering TSP and CVRP variants, asymmetric and multigraph distributions, time windows, multiple graph sizes, zero-shot scaling, up to ten parallel edges, and three-objective problems.

Results are consistently competitive with strong classical heuristics and substantially better than neural and evolutionary baselines in many settings. The large advantage on MGMOTSPTW particularly supports the value of learned edge selection when exact pruning is unavailable.

The learned-versus-simple-pruning, pre-pruning, architecture, augmentation, and generalization studies provide useful evidence for the proposed design choices. The manuscript also reports parameter counts, inference times, and training costs.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well written, with extensive appendices explaining architectures, distributions, baselines, and implementation choices.
weaknesses: All benchmark instances are synthetic. FLEX and FIX independently sample attributes and do not satisfy the triangle inequality, limiting evidence that performance transfers to realistic road-network multigraphs. Even one established or real-world dataset would materially strengthen the practical claims.

Experimental uncertainty is not reported: results appear to use a single trained model per configuration, with no variation across training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several claimed improvements are small enough that robustness cannot be assessed.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. No source-code or model-release commitment is stated, random seeds are absent, the ideal point used for Chebyshev training is not specified, and the precise normalization applied to hypervolume is unclear.

Runtime comparisons mix GPU inference for neural methods with CPU execution for classical solvers. Although hardware is disclosed, these figures do not establish hardware-normalized computational superiority; training is also expensive, reaching roughly 1.7 hours per epoch for GMS-EB on a 50-node multigraph.

The stated O(MN^4) decoding complexity for GMS-EB appears inconsistent with the description: scoring MN outgoing edges over N construction steps and N POMO trajectories suggests O(MN^3), absent an additional unreported factor. The complexity analysis should be corrected or derived more explicitly.

The strongest classical methods still achieve the best hypervolume on several core multigraph benchmarks, while the main advantage of GMS is amortized speed. This positioning is reasonable, but the manuscript occasionally overstates solution-quality superiority.

The time-window experiment is promising but uses a simplified soft-constraint formulation with no waiting or service time, and its baselines are relatively limited. Comparisons against a problem-specific routing heuristic or exact solver on smaller instances would better validate this central use case.
